utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel and everybody in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Ms. Laurie Sartorio, Matthias Neuner, and our case managers, Alma Imamovic and Fraser McIlwraith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friend from the Office of the Prosecutor and everyone in and around the courtroom. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Nicholas Robson, I appear on behalf of General Delic, with our legal assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. And good morning to you, sir, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. And just to warn you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, you are still cross-examining. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Husic. I hope you have rested. I won't take much longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the day before yesterday -- the day before yesterday we stopped working with -- when it was time for Exhibit 640 to be shown to the witness. The witness asked to be allowed to read the document. If it is easier for the witness, Your Honour, I can give him a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you read off the screen? Since it appears to be somewhat illegible, can you read that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a paper copy would do better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we have the English one pushed up. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down in the B/C/S, since I cannot see the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, now you can see the rest of the document. We've enlarged it; therefore, we were not able to see the signature block before.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the rest of the document in English, please. I'm trying to see the name of the person who signed. Thank you. "Name illegible." Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, as regards this document, you've already answered some questions. Your Honour -- His Honour asked you something about the first sentence, whereby several soldiers captured are mentioned, and here we have some information on one prisoner. It is true, is it not, is that this document by way of information was forwarded to the 37th Division, as the document reads?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was because the military unit that this soldier was serving with was from an area which was of interest for the 37th Division.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the document, one can see that the unit was engaged in the area of responsibility of the 37th Division.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that is the reason why you sent information to the 37th Division only on one this one person; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions concerning this document; perhaps the Bench may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to know to see whether the witness was able to recognise the signature, which according to the interpreters was illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have the signature in mind, I cannot recognise it. This is a truly poor copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise the name of the author anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the left-hand side from the signature block, it says: "MSA/AP," I believe. "MS" would stand for Mrkaljevic Sejfulah; therefore, he should be the author of the document. As regards the portion where the name cannot be seen, I have a somewhat better copy in -- on paper before me. Perhaps I can read it off that copy, but I cannot read it off the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please read it off the hard copy, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I be of assistance? We enlarged that version; therefore, on the hard copy, there is no signature block. We only enlarged the body of the text, but perhaps on the screen we can zoom in on the signature block itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't understand what you mean in the document, the hard copy doesn't have any signature block, ma'am. Is it the same paper? Is it the same document as we are seeing on the screen? Why doesn't it have that page which has a signature?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the enlarged copy -- the enlarged copy, Your Honour, that we received had no signature; however, the body of the text is exactly the same. If you wish, you can have a look at it. It is identical save for the signature block.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking for the enlarged copy. I'm just asking him to read from the hard copy the name of this person. The name of this person, even if there is no signature, must be there. The name of the author, not the drafter. The drafter he has told us is "MSC," but we want to know the person who takes ownership of this document. Are you able to find that name, sir, from the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the paper copy before me, that part is missing. You can see it for yourself, if you wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If you look at this enlarged document on the screen, are you able to make out the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a poor copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me. I had a question to the witness before we conclude this document. And my question is: Why was the information, information that was given by the witness -- by the prisoner of war, not passed on to the other units that took part in this same operation? Or to put my question in another way: What happened to the information that was offered by the other prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we can only see from this document that it was sent to the command of the 37th Division; however, that doesn't necessarily mean that information was not forwarded to other units in a different form, since we would usually send circular information on a weekly basis. What I can confirm based on this document is what is contained therein and what can be seen. As regards the second part of your question, also based on this document alone, I cannot confirm or say anything about other prisoners and whether such information was forwarded or not. If I was shown some other documents of that nature, perhaps I could be able to confirm something; but judging by this document alone, I cannot state that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, finally, was all of this information passed on to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was standard procedure that everything that was our -- at our disposal be forwarded to them; however, I can only repeat that by the looks of this document alone it was -- it seems only to have been sent to the command of the 37th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can put this document away. Could the witness be shown a document already shown by the Prosecutor. This is Exhibit 634.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a 3rd Corps command document of the intelligence department, dated the 9th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can scroll down so that the witness could see. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is your signature, is it not? That's what you've confirmed already.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also scroll down in the English, or perhaps could we focus on this part of the text. I meant to say the first paragraph of the text. Could both versions be centred so as to be able to see that part of the text. The English one as well. It is fine now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I wanted to draw your attention to this part of the document. This document speaks of the fact that the liberation has been concluded pertaining to the wider area of Seona, Stog, and Vozuca, and you've offered your comment. The next sends reads: "The establishment of an authority is underway in Vozuca, where there are around 200 MUP members." I'd like to ask you this: You received information that on that day, on the day of liberation of Vozuca, there were 200 MUP members who were trying to establish some sort of governance or authority.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The MUP is the Ministry of the Interior, meaning the civilian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These 200 members were assisting the military police of the 2nd and 3rd Corps in order to introduce some order; is that so?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This information is what was received by the intelligence administration of the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that 200 MUP members is a large number of policemen that arrived to introduce some order in the area?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fairly sizable number.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can move away from this document now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document. In your testimony, when responding to the Prosecutor's questions, some of them had to do with the El Mujahedin Detachment. Concerning that, I'd like to show you D588.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not D588. This is the document. Now it's on. Okay. Could the English version be focused.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a document of the Ministry of the Interior from Zenica. The date is 2nd September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please blow up the first half of the document for the witness, and the version in B/C/S. Thank you. Your Honour, I think it would be better for the witness to peruse the hard copy, because it's much clearer than the copy on the screen and it is also more complete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is the minutes of 2nd September, but the minutes concern a session that was held by the Ministry of the Interior in Zenica and the representatives of the military security of the 3rd Corps. Am I right in saying that? This session was held on the 28th of August, 1995, according to this document.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I can read in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And now I would like to ask you this: The third name from the top, Mr. Edo Husic, the assistant commander for intelligence, is that you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Is your nickname "Edo"? I apologise for asking you this.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they normally call me.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now will you agree that -- or do you agree, do you remember, first of all, that you attended a meeting at which you discussed the issues -- issue of citizens originating from African and Asian countries with the persons who are mentioned in this document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, but would you please allow me to read the document to remind myself of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly pay attention to the third page of that document and item 5, which is important for us as it concerns the detachment. The other bullet points do not concern the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Honourable Chamber, could the last page of the document be put on the screen for the Honourable Chamber's use.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Item 5 in this document says that: "The incidents involving persons from African and Asian countries. It is being said that those are members of the El Mujahid Detachment, which is arbitrary nation. And the conclusion is that measures should be taken, when such incidents are investigated involving persons from African and Asian countries, these persons should be identified." Do you remember whether you ever attended a meeting where such issues were discussed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is also stated herein that some malevolent persons spread rumours that all persons originating from African and Asian countries are members of the El Mujahid Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now what I would like to ask you is this: Did you personally hear, at least at that meeting, that there were several different groups of Arabs that acted in the territory of Central Bosnia in the course of 1995 independently of the El Mujahedin; i.e., of the El Mujahid Detachment?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can't remember the details of that meeting, but the fact remains that there were several people who hailed from those countries and arrived from those countries. It is absolutely certain that they were not all members of this El Mujahid Detachment, and it is also true that they were involved in certain incidents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, did you have information about some other groups, save for the El Mujahid Detachment, that were active in the territory of Central Bosnia? I'm not talking about individuals; I'm talking about groups, if you know.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, people from African and Asian countries mostly settled in the area around Travnik, in Mehurici, for example. That was one area in particular. I believe that there were also such people in the area of Zepce, in the general area of Zepce, rather than in town itself. I believe that there were some in the area of Tesanj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you this: Please, based on the discussion at this meeting, it seems that our state and military bodies could not tell the difference between these Arabs and that they were not in a position to tell who participated in certain incidents and that's why they insist on identifying these people. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a way you are. All of us in the BiH army wore uniforms and this was not their custom, so how could you tell a difference at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we do so, I would like to put a question relating to this document to the witness. Mr. Husic, why was there a need to identify particularly members of the El Mujahid Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to answer with any degree of precision, but it was very important to know who was creating problems when it came to public peace and order. From the intelligence point of view, since we were in charge of this activity, we were responsible for this activity. Contacts with members of foreign military and international organisations, it was very important for us to know what was happening, because every time you were in a situation, when you were told that this was done by the Mujahedin, it was very important for us, to put it that way, to know whether they were indeed members of the El Mujahid Detachment or some other -- others who only looked the same or looked that way. And why is that? Because if members of the El Mujahid Detachment were involved, then we were duty-bound to inform the commander; and if those people were civilians, then they were not our responsibility but, rather, the responsibility of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were the members of the El Mujahid Detachment known commonly to be particularly misbehaving against the local population? Was that the reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to give you an exact answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The other groups that you mentioned in Zepce and elsewhere, were they outside the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can say that they were not, but it all depended on the time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, then I don't understand the reason why it was important to have a meeting with the CSB in order to identify particularly the members of the El Mujahid Detachment, but you have given your answer to this question. I guess that there's not more information we can have about this point, so I suggest we move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, is it true that this document refers rather to incidents which was upsetting law and order, rather than behaviour patterns that occurred during combat activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one may put it that way. It was very important to know who is responsible and to make a distinction between the military part and the civilian part. The responsibilities had to be well-defined so as to take proper measures, and this was the goal of the meeting. If we were able to identify the perpetrators, then we knew who was responsible for them, but I can agree that what is mentioned here is mostly measures and violations of public peace and order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to do this. Could you explain to us what "CSB," "SJB," and "BVP" mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, "CSB" is Security Services Centre, which is a segment of the Ministry of the Interior; i.e., this is the civilian police. Here I can see "SJB," which is Public Security Service; although, I believe that in the document there should also be "SVB," which would be Military Security Service. As for the "BVP," that is the Battalion of the Military Police, the Military Police Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A little earlier, in response to an answer, you mentioned that you wore a uniform. What did you mean to imply by that? It is generally known that soldiers must wear a uniform. Why was it necessary to mention that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that because a lot of people from African and Asian countries wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did the El Mujahedin Detachment not to wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe they did, but I also believe that there were those who did not wear uniforms; although -- I apologise. If you're not on duty, if you had time off, then you did not have to wear a uniform. You were not duty-bound to wear a uniform on your free time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's applicable to everybody, all soldiers. All soldiers who are off duty didn't have to wear a uniform, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree with you; but for the purposes of identification, it was very important to identify all those who committed certain breaches or violations of law. But, generally speaking, people tended to believe that all those who hail from African and Asian countries were members of the El Mujahid. That's why we wanted to establish their identity, in order to be sure whether they indeed belonged to the El Mujahid Detachment or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a very straightforward question: When the El Mujahedin Detachment was in combat, did they wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer that, because I never participated in combat together with them. They should have, but I can't answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then, I don't understand why you referred to "uniform" a little earlier then. Why did you refer to "uniform," then, sir, if you don't know, because you used that word? The impression you left me with, let me tell you, was that the rest of the soldiers wear uniform and the El Mujahedin Detachment didn't. Now, if that is not what the impression you are wanting to give, can you tell us why you said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I used the word "uniform" because that was the most basic way to make a distinction between a soldier and a civilian; however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But my problem is where you said that an ordinary soldier, who is off duty and not wearing uniform, he's equally difficult to identify as a soldier, like it would be to identify an El Mujahedin Detachment member who's off duty and not wearing uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really did not understand this part. I said that uniform was and is something that distinguishes a soldier. But if somebody is off duty, they don't have to wear a uniform; and if they commit a breach of law, they have to be identified. Maybe I was misunderstood by you. Of course I mentioned "uniform," because that's the easiest way to tell the difference between a soldier and a civilian. I may have been misunderstood by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Then how did you then solve the problem that is mentioned in this document of making sure that you distinguish between members of the El Mujahedin Detachment and other members from African Arabic countries who were not members of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the document here, it says that it is necessary to identify persons; i.e., to establish their exact identity, the first name, the last name, irrespective of the clothes that they are wearing. In that case, if that person says that they are a member of the army, the civilian police had to refer the case to the military security or the military police, that will then be able to establish whether that person indeed exists on the list of army members. That's what I meant and that's what the document means when it says that persons who are wearing civilian clothes have to be identified. If, on the other hand, they are in uniform, then it's much easier to -- to do all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, did you come across any El Mujahedin Detachment member who was in uniform and was able to identify as one of yours by the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose I probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what uniform was he wearing, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember precisely any such moment, but it would have been customary for them to wear the uniform with a pattern that was worn by us at the time in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the question. It would have been customary to do so. So my question to you really is did they; and if you don't know, say so. If you don't know, say you don't know. I want to know what actually happened on the ground. Did they wear uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put just one more question to you. Sir, in addition to thinking that they did, did you actually see them in combat? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I did not see them in combat, so I cannot confirm any answers to such questions. As far as this document is concerned, neither I nor the Department for Intelligence had the obligation to establish identification. That was not my duty. So even if I had encountered somebody, it was just by accident at that particular moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any other questions. I would kindly ask for this document to be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. But the answer to your very last question raises a question in me. When you say it's neither yours or the Department of Intelligence's obligation to establish identification, then what intelligence did you collect, sir? If you can't begin to be able to distinguish between your own members and those who are not your members, because the El Mujahedin Detachment was part of you, what intelligence were you collecting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, obviously, we're talking at cross-purposes here. Our forces were not a subject of work or interest of the intelligence services. It was rather the enemy forces that were the subject of our interest. However, the intelligence department of the 3rd Corps was in charge of contacts with foreign armies and international organisations that arrived with their questions, statements, with their agenda, to put it that way. It was very important for us to have information about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. I'm sorry. You're going too far. I hear what you're saying, that your forces were not subject or interest of the intelligence but, rather, the enemy was. But how do you know who is your enemy if you don't know who your own members are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, Your Honours. That's why there is the military intelligence service that is involved with our forces. That's what you call counter-intelligence. When they get hold of information and when this information concerns the enemy forces, then it will be customary for them to refer that information to us. That -- what was important for us was the enemy that was beyond the contact line. If there was an enemy infiltrated within our lines, then it would be the security services who would be concerned with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can't take the question any further. Any re-examination, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you go for your re-examination, document D588 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 641.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Husic. I have just a few questions relating to a document which you have seen on Tuesday by my learned friend, as well as by myself. It is Exhibit 630.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't think there's a need to put it up right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: It's the plan for intelligence support, and you explained to us it is relating to Operation Farz. This is on page 70 of Tuesday's transcript. You were asked by my learned friend about the axis Svinjasnica-Paljenic-Stog-Miljevici-Vozuca. You will remember this. And in response to her question, you said: "Given that this document is a working draft, any part of the document may be subject to changes, to alterations." Do you recall having said that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Who could make such changes or alterations?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For us to be able to do our part of the work, we were supposed to be provided with a general idea, general concept that was supposed to have been provided by the commander. As regards our part of the planning, we can introduce changes and alterations to the document if there were some changes which went against the initial or general concept. Another possible thing is that given that this was a working version, all alterations were possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to pick up on your answer. You say you could get from the commander some suggestions. Which commander are you referring to? Could you name him?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one commander, that of the 3rd Corps. At the time, it was Brigadier Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So, if Brigadier Mahmuljin would suggest a change in your plan for intelligence support, who in fact would make the change in the working document?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be made by us, the intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So would you know about any change being made to your plan for intelligence support?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot understand the question fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We were discussing changes -- possible changes to the working draft, which is called "Plan for Intelligence Support," which you had seen. My question to you was: If any such questions were made, if you as the head, the assistant commander of the intelligence department of the 3rd Corps, would you know if changes were made to this working plan?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay. Having that established, could you tell me: You drew for us the axis Svinjasnica-Paljenic-Stog-Miljevici-Vozuca on the map. At the time, was this axis for intelligence support, this focus of intelligence support changed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor led the witness when marking the axis; therefore, he cannot now start by saying that the witness marked the axis. He did, but he was led by the Prosecutor. It didn't come about because the witness was indeed claiming that that particular axis was subject to the operational plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can withdraw the part of my question relating to the map itself, but my question could in essence be the same. Since the witness has told us that he would know any changes to be made to the working plan, I can ask him without touching upon the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, we discussed the focus of the axis for intelligence support in the wider Vozuca area on the basis of a working plan. My question to you is: Did you at the time become aware that this axis had changed before the document was finally adopted?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. In any case, Vozuca was within our area of interest. I cannot confirm what the exact axis was, unless I am given a document from which I can read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But could you at least confirm whether you had to make changes or not.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that either. Anything that is ordered or anything that we were told to do we did. Since you're asking me about this specific example, without other supporting documentation, I cannot say anything for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Neuner. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a general question to ask from you, but now it comes from a question which was asked by the Defence this morning. I would like to have some clarification concerning the status of the civilian police during wartime, the civilian police who belongs to the MUP. During wartime there was a cooperation or collaboration between civil police, MUP, and military police, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is not clear for me is whether there was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but during wartime there were the armed forces who included also the civilian police. Could you please enlighten us on this point.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you this: It is my understanding that the forces of the civilian police were not part of the 3rd Corps; therefore, the commander had -- held no authority over them. The municipal chief did, though, or rather, anyone who was directing and controlling and ordering them. I cannot confirm therefore anything in relation to your question concerning the armed forces. It is a fact that the commander did not issue orders to those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say the commander of the 3rd Corps or the commander of the Bosnian army? Which are you saying?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, if we are talking about the units of the civilian police -- well, we had the military police. They were part and parcel of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were directly linked to the commander; however, the civilian police was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that they were different institutions; but in wartime, during wartime, these two, were they cooperating and making a sort of joint institution, a single institution called armed forces or something like that? Was it the case, if I remember rightly, therefore permitting a cooperation to fight against the enemy during wartime?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can agree with your hypothesis; however, I can confirm to you that the 3rd Corps commander did not issue orders or control the forces of the civilian police which, for example, were in the town of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in asking this question, I was not asking that relating to your own functions of assistant to the information department, but in your functions as a military who has been to a military academy. So, maybe, in the military academy, you were told how during wartime this will work in the general defence of the country and who are the organs who are directly engaged in this common defence. But if you have -- if you can't answer me, this will do.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tried to tell you about the situation to the extent of the things I knew, irrespective of what I learned or did not learn at the military academy. As far as I know, I never saw the commander order anything to the civilian police. They had nothing to do with the 3rd Corps command, and we held no authority over them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Husic, you will have understood that your testimony here is particularly relevant to the issue of the registration of prisoners of war and also for the information of what happened to these prisoners of war that were taken by the ABiH during the war and, in particular, during the Vozuca operation in September 1995. Last Tuesday you testified about this, and you told us that information had been received by the 3rd Corps, and that there was, after the liberation of the area down in the southern part of the Vozuca pocket - I believe it was the Prokop area, around Kamenica, the Kablovac-Stoska area - reports had been made that there were, I think you called it, broken-up groups of Chetnik soldiers still roaming around in the woods. One information was passed on by the 2nd Corps and another information came from the 3rd Corps, your own corps, and the groups were in one case a group of 40 to 60 Chetnik soldiers, and the other information was a group of 50 Chetnik soldiers. I believe we also heard Tuesday from you that there was possibly a third group of 100 Chetnik soldiers. I remember we asked you Tuesday if the information that was received by your unit was information that really concerned one and the same group, that altogether there was perhaps a group of Chetnik soldiers running around out there approximately of the size of somewhere between 40 to 100 soldiers. You told us that you couldn't say for sure because at that moment, when these documents were written, the information was only preliminary, and there was no final assessment of how many people we were really talking about out there in the woods. My question to you now is: Were the 3rd Corps ever able to establish how many Chetnik soldiers were left behind enemy lines after the liberation of the Vozuca pocket, and do you know what happened to these people? How many of them were actually taken prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, for us, the people of the intelligence department, POWs were merely a source of information. The information gained through interviews with them need not to have been correct. Within the intelligence department, we did not keep any record of their numbers, and we did not follow through in order to establish what happened to them. They were only important to us to conduct an interview in order to obtain some data which may be of assistance and which are of intelligence interest. I cannot confirm what the number was. I cannot tell you how many there were or were not; therefore, from that point of view, I cannot be of assistance to you. It was our priority to have what they had stated at our disposal. As for the rest, they fell under the competence of the military police and the military security service. The intelligence branch held no obligation towards them. If we are talking about this specific case, since your question was rather long, I cannot tell you anything precisely. There is data in the intelligence reports pertaining to prisoners of war, and that was the extent of information we had processed. As for any other information, I cannot be held responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise for having spoken at length. The reason was just that I wanted to provide you with a bit of background for my question. To put it shortly, then: How many prisoners of war did you talk to after the Vozuca operation? Roughly just. You don't need to tell us any specific numbers; but to your recollection, what are we speaking about? 20 people? 40 people? Please give us your estimation of the number of persons that you were questioning after the operation.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, based on my recollection, I cannot tell you precisely, not even a rough estimate. If there were interviews conducted at lower levels, this is where our interest in them ceased; therefore, I truly cannot answer to your question. I don't know what the exact number would be, and I cannot even offer an estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sir, with all respect, I accept that you would be unable to provide an estimation of the total number of prisoners that were taken during the Vozuca operation, but I believe that you should be able to tell us approximately how many of these prisoners of war that you spoke to, that you were actually questioning and seeking information from. I realise that it's a long time ago, but you must be able to have some sort of an idea of how many people you spoke to.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to be more precise. As far as I recall, I personally did not interview anyone. As far as I recall, during that time in that department, we never kept any figures. I am truly sorry, but I cannot even estimate in answering your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe it's time for the break, so let's adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take an adjournment and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, as a man, as an officer of intelligence, I am sure that you did hear rumours at the time about how many Chetnik soldiers were left in the area in September 1995. Did you hear any such rumours, and can you tell us what you heard?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really cannot confirm that there is anything that could confirm that existence. For us in the intelligence department, I can't really say that it didn't mean anything; but for us, it was important to complete our part of the job; i.e., to carry out interviews with all prisoners of war. As for any rumours, we really were not concerned with any of that. The information that we had was put in our reports. I really can't remember, and I really can't answer your question in a positive way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have maybe one or two questions to you. One specific issue that I want to raise with you, sir, and let me just say I raise this issue with you because you mentioned that you went to the military academy. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the question really doesn't arise from what you have been testifying about, but I just want to find out from your knowledge as a person who has been to the academy just to cast light, if you can. We have heard evidence here, and what I'm going to say is subject to confirmation by the parties. I would like them to listen carefully; and if I am wrong, correct me. But in the El Mujahedin Detachment, really no numbers could be given, but there are some times when we have heard numbers of between 600 and 800 and, if I'm not mistaken, really not beyond 1.000. Would it be normal, if that is the number generally, more or less, is it normal within the structure of an army for a unit of that size to be subordinated to a corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away. I cannot see a link between my education and your question, and let me explain that by saying this: The education that would enable one to work for higher commands also implying -- implied the completion of command staff school. So we can easily say that the military academy did offer some knowledge that sufficed for an officer to eventually become a battalion commander. Everything above that would have required additional education. Obviously, since there was a lack of personnel and given the circumstances, and also in light of the fact that I had completed the education that I did, I am absolutely sure that there were other -- if there had been other officers with intelligence education, my position would have been filled with somebody else. It would not have been my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's not go on for too long. Okay. I understand and I'm sorry if I'm asking you a question that is not covered by your education; but, you see, I think the problem is that I have no military education at all, so I'm trying to get information here. Let's put aside your education, then. Let's look at the structure of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as it was at the time. Would you agree that the El Mujahedin Detachment was the smallest unit in number subordinated to a corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer that question because I really don't know what the strength of that particular unit was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I did say is we have heard evidence that nobody really knew what the strength of that unit was, but I've given you ballpark figures of what we have heard so far, which I said are subject to the confirmation by the parties if I am wrong. Working on that ballpark figure that I gave, would that be a large enough unit to be directly subordinated to a corps?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is just my opinion. It may have been the case. I believe that there were some staff units that were linked to the corps that were even of a lower strength, and I believe that at times there were even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give an example?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An example of such a unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All staff units; for example, the signals company, the reconnoitering company. Their strength was lower, and they were all linked with the corps command. When I say that their strength was lower, those units usually numbered anything between 60 and 100 men. It all depended on the characteristics of those units. But, as I've already said, I really can't and I don't know anything about the strength of any other unit. I really can't answer your question with any precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you saying that those units were subordinated directly to the corps? They didn't come -- they were not subordinated to the corps via battalions and brigades and what have you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me give you an example. For example, the sabotage unit that was some 100 men strong was directly linked to the corps, and the command was the one who decided how to use the unit, whether to resubordinate it to somebody or engage that unit independently; in other words, there were units that were directly linked to the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those are units which were doing specialised work like sabotages, as you say, not general combat work.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this takes me back to the question we discussed a few minutes ago, before we went on break, the question of uniform. You see, we have heard testimony here - again, I'm subject to correction by the parties - that the El Mujahedin Detachment did not wear uniform.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't say that in that sense. I said that I couldn't confirm with any degree precision. I was never in that unit, and I said that they should have had. I was never with them either during combat or at any other time, so how can I say whether they did or they didn't? I suppose that they should have had them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. We are probably talking at cross-purposes, you and I. Understand, I'm not trying to challenge your testimony. I understand that you are saying they should have. I'm talking about what actually happened on the ground. You don't know what happened on the ground because, as you have just explained, you were never with them in combat, so you never saw them in combat. I understand that, but all I'm saying to you is -- and understand when I asked you this question about uniform earlier, it's because you had used the word, and I just wanted to get confirmation from you if you knew. Now you are saying you don't know. I'm saying that there are those who claim to know, who have testified before the Tribunal in this case, who have told us that the El Mujahedin Detachment did not wear uniform. I wanted to say to you if -- Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, if I may. The testimonies in that sense, especially by members of the El Mujahid Detachment, differed to a large extent, and the gist of their testimony may be reduced to them saying -- some said that they did wear uniforms; some said that they didn't, if I may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may be so --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Correction: Some did wear uniforms and some didn't wear uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That may be so, but all the other members of other units of the army, when in combat, wore uniform. That's right. Now, that's the point I'm making. There is this distinction. It seems to me as if, right from the beginning, the El Mujahedin Detachment was treated differently from the rest of the army. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say, when we are talking about this issue, is that we in the intelligence department did not have any contacts with them. I don't know whether they had an intelligence man among them. They never sent us any reports. There were no contacts on our part. That's as much as I can tell you when it comes to that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's a further point of distinction between that detachment and the rest of the units. And because of that, just what you have just said, would you agree that they seem to have been treated differently from other units of the army? Some wore uniforms, some didn't. They didn't have an intelligence department that reported to you. They never gave any reports to you, and everybody else was given reports. We've seen orders here that whenever orders are given to subordinates, it's an order. When they relayed to the El Mujahedin, they are asked to do things in conjunction with the El Mujahedin. They must consult the leadership of the Mujahedin. They seem to have been treated different. Wouldn't you agree, sir? This seems to -- yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am really concerned about this question. The actions that you've just described may imply other sort of behaviour on the part of the unit and not that their attitude towards them was different. That's why I'm kindly asking you to -- to bear that in mind as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are saying, Madam Vidovic, because I'm not talking about the actions of the Mujahedin. I'm talking about the actions of the army towards the Mujahedin, how the army treated the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with all due respect, the witness can talk about his attitude or the attitude of his unit and his command in that sense, and that's why I believe that the question is really -- I appreciate that the Bench may put questions in order to deal with some factual issues, but I'm very concerned with the fact that this is a very leading question that goes beyond the framework of the witness's possible knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I'm just going on asking this witness to comment on the facts that have been led before this Tribunal, and I did say at the beginning that I'm not dealing specifically with things arising from his testimony, but I'm asking him these questions because of his -- what I thought to be his specialised knowledge because of having to have been to the academy. He said the information has nothing to do with his schooling. But I am now telling him the facts that we have been told, and I'm asking him to comment. I can't understand what your problem is. You know, all I'm asking him to say is whether in his view would he -- given the facts that I've put to him, does he agree that the El Mujahedin Detachment was treated differently. It was not a specialised unit like a sabotage unit, yet it was a small unit. It was subordinated right from the beginning to the 3rd Corps. Some didn't wear uniform. They, as he says, they had no intelligence department. Can't anybody comment, given those facts? That's all I'm asking him to do. Sir, are you able to make a comment given those facts? There are many others I could give you that I won't give you, but those three: They are subordinated to the corps, the fact that they some of them didn't wear uniform, and the fact that, as you say, they just didn't send intelligence reports to you. They were treated differently, were they not? If you don't know, sir, you don't know; if you know, sir, you know. Or rather, if you agree, say you agree; and if you don't agree, you don't have to agree.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as my views are concerned, I've already told you that I did not have any contacts with that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not receive from them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Just understand the distinction between a view and fact. It is fact that you didn't have contact with them. Now, I'm giving you that fact back to you, and I'm saying: Does the fact that you didn't have contact with them indicate that in fact they were treated differently, because you had contact with others.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at things from that point of view, I can say that, as far as I'm concerned, they did not carry out their obligations, that they did not comply with their obligations. I asked for the 35th Division to report on them as well, to include them in the information that they were privy to. That's what you can read in one of my documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, now, you're now moving into an area which I wasn't in, talking about them complying with their obligations. I'm talking about them complying with their obligations, number one; number two, yes, I understand that they were at some stage re-subordinated to the 35th Division, but at some stage they were also subordinated directly to the 3rd Corps. At that time, when they were directly subordinated to the 3rd Corps, they gave you no reports, did they? You've told us that.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the very fact that they didn't have any intelligence department in their unit, does this -- what does this mean to you, given the fact that every unit had to have that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I don't know what their composition was. I don't know whether they had an intelligence department or not. I only know that they did not submit any reports. As far as I'm concerned, we did not have any contacts with that unit. As for the control of that unit, I can't tell you anything about that because the commander was the one who was in charge of the command of all the units. I am referring to the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to answer specifically to the question that I am putting to you, which is: Would you agree that they were treated differently? If you don't -- I'm not forcing you to agree but I'm just asking you: Are you able to answer to that question? Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm really concerned that you keep insisting on the witness answering this question because this question goes directly to establishment of the elements of guilt. It doesn't arise at all from the previous testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I think I've explained myself and I'm ruling you out of order. Sir, are you able to answer my question? "Yes, I'm able," "no, I'm not able," and I'll stop.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that they didn't submit a reports, they were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen my question. Are you able to answer my question? "Yes, I'm able to answer you," or "no, I'm not able to answer you." Don't try to answer that -- what you are now saying is what I'll asking you depending on what you say to this one question that I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, could you then please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is: Are you able to answer my question? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give it my best shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Give it your best shot. Do you want me to remind you what the question was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: Would you agree that they were treated differently or not?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I'm in a position to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You have answered me. You should have long done that. Thank you. Any questions arising from the questions from the Bench? Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to follow up a little bit on the lines of questioning by Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: He had asked you about the presence of enemy soldiers in the wider Vozuca pocket. I'm not interested in the numbers, since they were given in the documents we discussed. I'm more interested in the direction of their flight. You had explained to us that the Vozuca pocket was cut off through convergence of 2nd Corps coming from the east and 3rd Corps coming from the western side and they had met. Could you explain to the Chamber in which general direction were Serb soldiers, who were cut off by convergence of 2nd and 3rd Corps, in which general direction were Serb soldiers trying to flee?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. If there is a report where I could read this, maybe I could confirm the contents of such a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to follow up on the questions put to the witness by Her Honour Lattanzi.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you remember that Judge Lattanzi asked you about the status of the civilian police and the attitude of the civilian police -- or rather, the relationship between the army and the civilian police? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, I would like to ask you this: You are a member of the armed forces, aren't you? You were a member, rather, of the armed forces, and you can answer my next question: Will you agree with me that this issue was resolved by the decree on the Armed Forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that there are, in other words, regulations dealing with that issue?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: I can't give you any detail without the document before my eyes. I told you how things were in practice. I was never in the position to see the commander issuing any orders to the civilian police, nor were any links between my service and the civilian police that would give us authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you something else now. Please, do you agree with me that the civilian police was under the authority of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EDIN HUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No further questions. That is the end of your testimony, sir. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Travel well back home. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you calling the next witness, Mr. Robson?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Your Honour, it's just a matter of clarification, if I may. It relates to the question that you put to the witness relating to uniforms, and you said that was subject to confirmation from the parties. Obviously, Madam Vidovic gave you some information about evidence that we heard from Mujahedin members, and I'd just like to state for the record that in relation to certainly one of the Serb victim victims that testified, Mr. Trivicevic. At page 3601, lines 7 to 11, he stated that: "In respect of the Mujahedin, they weren't all wearing the same type of uniform. They even were wearing some civilian clothes, bits and pieces of civilian clothing items. In a manner of speaking, different types of uniform." So I just wanted to put that on record, Your Honour, that there was other evidence as well suggesting there were a mixture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That confirms what we were told by Madam Vidovic, that some were, some were not. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. I wanted to leave the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone please, when you speak, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I apologise. I just wanted to leave the courtroom to make space for my colleagues to lead the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We will call the next witness, Mr. Goran Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Good morning. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, as -- as Your Honours know, we have proposed that this witness be 92 ter, and we have reached an agreement, I believe, with Defence counsel with regard to the admissibility of this witness's previous statements. I'll just ask the witness some preliminary questions about those statements, and then we will ask that they be omitted -- I mean, excuse me, that they be admitted into evidence with minus certain paragraphs that we have agreed would be deleted, or however Your Honours want to -- want us to handle it: Whether you want us to submit redacted statements or just ignore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you should submit the redacted statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. We won't have those today. We will substitute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: My name is Goran Krcmar.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I was born on the 12th of February, 1963.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in what municipality and country do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I currently reside in Banja Luka in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in -- what is your current occupation, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Currently, I worked for the governmental office for the missing persons of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long did -- have you worked in that governmental office?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I've been working there since 1996, since April that year.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And just one more question about this: What -- do you have a title or a position there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I am the office clerk of the commission. We are in charge of the missing persons who had gone missing during the war in Central Bosnia and Posavina area.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your capacity in this position, have you provided a written statement or statements to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I gave statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And let's talk about the first statement. Do you recall the date of your first statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I think it was in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I'd like the witness to be shown P06195, and for -- I have hard copies, which I understand is procedure 92 ter, so he can look at the entire statement. I don't know if that's appropriate, but would the Court allow me to give a hard copy of his statement to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you to the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, I've just given you a copy of what I'm going to ask you about; and, also, you can see on the screen in front of you the first page of a document in English and the Bosnian. Is this the first statement that you gave to OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Would you agree that this statement was dated -- is dated 21st December 2005?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: You are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I rise to my feet just to say that the -- what is on our screen is the statement from the 6th of June, 2007. I'm content for my learned friend to lead on the dates of these statements and obviously that they're going to be introduced into evidence, so there's --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I meant P06194. I said "95," but I was thinking 2005, so if we could have 6194. I apologise. Can you -- is the B/C/S -- I can't see the date on the Bosnian version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay, sir, I apologise. What is the date of this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The date is the 21st of December, 2005. This is the first of the two statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And is this your statement, sir, that you gave to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can he see the signature --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. That would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- before he confirms that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. May we see the signature page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And ask him about the signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Looking at the first page of the English, sir, is that your signature, at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And in a moment I'm going to show you the last page so you can confirm that that is the last page of -- of your statement, if it is, and that's your signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But I will proceed with questions, if I may, Your Honour, assuming it is his signature. I don't see it on my screen. Oh, okay. Sorry. I apologise. I'm not -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you provided this written statement, did you answer the questions of the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And did you answer these questions freely; that is, without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I've answered all of the questions freely.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, at the conclusion of this interview in December of 2005, your statement was actually typed in English, and was it read back to you in your language, the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Yes. The statement was read back to me in Bosnian, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get to that, because that was recently. So did you -- originally, though, did you sign this statement in English?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I think I signed the English version and I received the translation somewhat later. I was able to notice that there were some changes made there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say "sometime later," was that -- can you give us a time frame? Was that recently?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Some two months ago or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. And the changes that were made - and I'm going to show you that statement as well - was that also read and signed by you? Does -- you don't understand my question, sir?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I still cannot see those changes on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. May the witness please be shown P06196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you want to do with P06194 in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I'll ask that it be admitted; but if -- the witness has -- is discussing changes that he made, I want to make sure that he know it is changes were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is the point. We can't admit something to which he say there is are changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's right. That's why I'm going to ask to put this aside, and I'll show the witness 6196 for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Could we move down to the bottom of the page, please, to see ...

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, now, there's a document in front of you. Can you identify what this document is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: The document I signed dated the 6th October 2007 contains the changes in relation to the first, original statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: I believe those changes had to do with translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown page 1 in both English and Bosnian -- excuse me, page 2, the first page of the statement actually, substantive. To the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, sir, at the top of this document, if you would read --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: If the B/C/S version could be moved up, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, this -- could you tell us what -- the paragraph number 1, does it refer to changes that you're making in this document to two statements?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: Precisely so. This is my statement by the virtue of which I tried to enumerate the corrections I wanted to make to the two statements. Each of the paragraphs contains a correction that needs to be introduced. For example, the cover page, it states that I speak both Serbian and English; whereas, it should only read "Serbian."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KRCMAR
utterances.text: And it goes on by the paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Can -- may the witness be shown the last page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the statement containing the changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, we ask that P06196 be admitted into evidence, as well as P06194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are these -- yes, Mr. Robson. First, let's hear you first.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before these statements are admitted into evidence, I think it's important for the Prosecution to put on record which paragraphs it has been agreed between the parties have been redacted, have been removed from the statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was actually going to ask her --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
